planting.note: Divide established clumps or pot up bulbil-raised plantlets in spring and set into humus-rich, well-drained soil with the crown just above grade.

directions: This old Victorian-era selection of the soft shield fern is distinguished by narrower, more elegantly tapered fronds with short, splayed side pinnae rather than the broad, lax shape of the typical species. It forms a slow-growing, evergreen to semi-evergreen rosette and, like other Polystichum setiferum selections, often sets small plantlet bulbils along the rachis that can be detached and grown on. Site it in dappled to full shade in soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, and mulch lightly to protect the crown over winter in colder parts of its range. It pairs well with hellebores and hostas in a woodland border.

planting.note: Transplant divisions or fall-formed frond bulbils into loose, humus-rich soil in part to full shade in spring, keeping the crown proud of the soil surface.

directions: One of the most dissected of all the soft shield fern selections, this Victorian-era find builds a dense, layered mound of triple- and quadruple-pinnate fronds so finely cut that mature plants take on a soft, moss-like texture rather than a typical fern silhouette. In autumn it frequently forms tiny viviparous plantlets along the mature fronds, an easy means of increase in addition to crown division. Grow it in consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part to full shade, and cut back tattered fronds in late winter to let the new flush unfurl cleanly. It is slower and more compact than the species, making it well suited to shaded containers or path edges.

planting.note: Set divisions into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in bright to full shade in spring; this dwarf form is well suited to raised beds and containers where drainage is assured.

directions: A dwarf, tightly congested sport of the soft shield fern, this cultivar packs its overlapping pinnae close along a short, upright rachis and finishes each frond tip in a mildly tasseled crest. The compact habit stays under a foot tall and wide, making it one of the more restrained Polystichum setiferum forms for small shaded rock gardens or container plantings. It is evergreen to semi-evergreen and wants moist but freely draining soil enriched with leaf mold; shelter from drying winter wind keeps the crested fronds looking tidy into the following spring. Increase by careful division of the crown rather than by seed to retain the crested form.

planting.note: Use only nursery-propagated stock, never wild-collected material, and tuck divisions into cool, humid, alkaline rocky soil in deep shade in spring.

directions: This federally threatened North American variety of the hart's-tongue fern survives in only a handful of cool, humid limestone and dolomite sinkholes and talus slopes scattered from Alabama and Tennessee north to Michigan, New York, and Ontario. Its undivided, strap-shaped evergreen fronds have a heart-shaped lobed base and a glossy texture distinct from the finely cut fronds of most garden ferns. In cultivation it demands constant atmospheric humidity, alkaline rocky soil, cool root temperatures, and deep, steady shade approximating its native sinkhole habitat, conditions difficult to replicate outside a shaded rock garden with limestone scree. Because wild populations are protected, only responsibly propagated nursery stock should ever be planted.
sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service Species Profile

planting.note: Wedge divisions into gritty, sharply drained soil between rocks in part sun to light shade in spring, mimicking the cliff-crevice habitat this fern needs.

directions: Endemic to dry, exposed sandstone, granite, and gneiss cliffs and outcrops of the southern and central Appalachians and the Ozarks, this small deciduous fern forms tight basal clumps of lacy, twice-cut light green fronds only a few inches tall. It is closely allied to the western Rocky Mountain cliff fern and is treated by some botanists as its own species. In the garden it performs best in a crevice garden or dry rock wall with sharp drainage and part sun to light shade rather than a conventional moist shade bed, and it goes dormant in winter after fronds die back. Avoid rich, wet soils, which quickly rot the shallow root system.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Nestle rhizome divisions into thin, moss-covered soil pockets on rock or atop a lean, sharply drained bed in spring, pressing the creeping rhizome just under the surface.

directions: Native to rock outcrops and boulder fields across boreal Canada and Alaska, this cold-hardy polypody is one of the parent species of the common eastern rockcap fern and is itself a tough, creeping choice for a shaded rock garden. Narrow, pinnatifid evergreen fronds arise singly along a slender, branching rhizome that spreads slowly over mossy stone or thin, gritty soil. It tolerates far colder winters than most garden ferns and prefers a lean, sharply drained site over rich garden loam, making it a good match for a shaded boulder or crevice planting rather than a conventional border. Established rhizome mats can be divided and moved in spring with minimal disturbance.
